Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital payment systems.  21 variables in 4 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: AfricaNenda SIIPS 2022 shows SYRAD does not meet the “pro-poor governance” criterion in its inclusivity assessment table (criterion not checked for SYRAD), and no public evidence was found of end-user/consumer representation or explicit inclusion mandate in SYRAD governance. ([AfricaNenda SIIPS 2022](https://www.africanenda.org/uploads/files/EN_SIIPS_Report_web.pdf))
revision_notes: Original SIIPS 2022 citation checked and confirmed: SYRAD is not flagged as meeting the pro-poor governance criterion in AfricaNenda's inclusivity assessment. Cross-checked against SIIPS 2023 (SYRAD again not ranked as meeting basic inclusivity criteria, including pro-poor governance) and SIIPS 2024, which removed SYRAD from the IPS landscape entirely because it does not fulfil the definitional requirements for a live, fully operational inclusive payment system. The Banque Centrale de Djibouti's own description of SYRAD (RTGS/ACH launched July 2021) shows the BCD as owner, supervisor and operator, with participants engaging only as direct/indirect settlement participants and no consumer advisory, small-provider representation, or financial inclusion mandate evident in its governance structure. No authoritative source contradicts the original 'No' score; confirmed unchanged. Newest reliable evidence is the SIIPS 2024 report (data collected to June 2024).
revised_comments: Djibouti's payment settlement system, SYRAD (Système de Règlement Automatisé de Djibouti), is operated by the Banque Centrale de Djibouti, which acts as the system's owner, supervisor and operator. Its governance structure provides no explicit pro-poor mechanisms: there is no consumer advisory body, no reserved representation for small payment service providers, and no stated financial inclusion mandate in its governing rules. AfricaNenda's State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems reports consistently find that SYRAD does not meet the pro-poor governance criterion used to assess inclusivity across African instant payment systems, and the 2024 edition removes SYRAD from the inclusive payment systems landscape altogether because it does not meet the definitional requirements of a fully operational, inclusive system.
